    Introduction

    This course introduces the eLabFTW API and how to use it. It is designed for researchers who want to interact with their eLabFTW instance programmatically. As such, you should be familiar with using eLabFTW through it’s user interface (UI).

    Since this course is supposed to reach as many researchers as possible, it does contain some very basic concepts on APIs, Python, and Jupyter Notebooks. Bear with us here if you are already familiar with these concepts. We will also code some short example scripts that act upon the data so we can work through a mildly realistic sceanario.

    Notes and Resources

    We have joint notepad for this course. Feel free to job things down:

    Content from The eLabFTW API

    Last updated on 2026-10-13 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 15 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What is a (REST) API?
    • What can I do with the eLabFTW API
    • Where can I find help on the eLabFTW API
    • How can I write and API call?
    • How can I view the response?

    Objectives

    • explain what a (REST) API is (in very basic terms)
    • explain what they can do with the eLabFTW API
    • find help on the eLabFTW API
    • formulate the API URL for a given eLabFTW instance
    • make a basic eLabFTW API call using the browser
    • interpret eLabFTW API responses

    Introduction to APIs

    In this course, we will be using the eLabFTW API to interact with the ELN. First, though, let’s take a step back and clarify what APIs are.

    API is short for application programming interface. You may also see the term REST or RESTful API, which indicates that an API conforms to design principles of the representational state transfer (REST) architectural style.

    An API, or application programming interface, is a set of rules or protocols that enables software applications to communicate with each other to exchange data, features and functionality. (https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/api)

    A (REST) API is, simply put, something that allows you to (programmatically) interface an application.

    Let’s use an analogy from the real world: a restaurant.

    Image generated by RWTHgpt, model: OpenAI FPT Image-1-mini

    Restaurant | Software:

    • In a restaurant, the guests want food, which the kitchen can provide.
    • In a software system, one application wants information that another can provide.

    Waiter | API:

    • In a restaurant, the waiter takes your order to the kitchen and brings back your food.
    • In software, the API receives your request and provides the appropriate response.

    Menu | Documentation:

    • In a restaurant, there is a menu that describes which food is available at which cost.
    • In software, the documentation describes what the API can provide and how.

    Kitchen | Server:

    • In a restaurant, there is the kitchen with its staff to provide food for guests.
    • In software, the server and its processes provide data to users.

    Table | Application:

    • In a restaurant, the guests sit at the table to interact with the food from the kitchen they get from the waiter.
    • In software, the user uses an application to work with data from a server provided by its API.

    The eLabFTW API

    eLabFTW’s API let’s you interact with the ELN, e.g., retrieve and write information from it, without using the graphical user interface (GUI). This is something you may want to do to create automated workflows and avoid repetitive work.

    Sticking with our restaurant analogy, we first need to figure out what is available to us, in programmatic terms: what requests we may make (or in restaurant terms: what orders we may place).

    To this end, we head to the menu, or in the API’s case, the documentation, or short docs:

    This gives us very basic information on the API. If we scroll down we find another link to the full documentation.

    Three things are important for this course: (1) the version 2 documentation link, which leads to the APIs Swagger documentation page, (2) the HTML doc (v2) and (3) the Python Library (v2) link, the latter two of which we will get to later.

    Let’s head to the Swagger page. Here, we have a list of endpoints, sub-divided into categories. Each link is color-coded to indicate the type of request, further marked by PUT, POST, GET, PATCH, and DELETE labels.

    Scrolling through the categories and knowing how eLabFTW is structured, we can get a pretty good idea of the types of interaction we can carry out. For instance, under Experiment Categories we have a GET request that let’s us read all experiment categories in a given team (indicated by it’s ID).

    Constructing Requests

    The first time you see these types of docs pages, it may seem a bit daunting. So let’s construct our first API call using a tool we’re all familiar with: our browser.

    1. Write the eLabFTW URL, e.g., https://elab.parks.web.gateway.ionos.coscine.dev or https://research.eln.rwth-aachen.de in the menu bar.
    2. Add /api/v2.
    3. Add /users/me, behind this (hint: for more complicated endpoints, copy and paste from docs by hovering over the endpoint and using the clipboard icon).
    4. You show now have something that looks http://elab.parks.web.gateway.ionos.coscine.dev/api/v2/users/me.
    5. Hit return.

    If you are not logged in, you will get a 401 error since you are not authorized to view this information. Log in to eLabFTW, then refresh the page.

    Challenge

    Find your User ID

    What is your user ID? Find it and note for later.

    The top line has the userid attribute, which is your user ID. You can also use the browser’s search function to find it: ctrl+f → type ‘userid’.

    Requests typically return JSON. Depending on which browser you are using, it may be rendered nicely for better readability. Understanding the structure can greatly help when you are trying to find a specific piece of information. What helpful is knowing which key the value you are looking for belongs to. userid was the key in our example.

    We can also see a nested structure when we look at the teams key, with more keys provided for each team listed.

    Key Points
    • An API lets us interact with software in a programmatic manner
    • The APIs docs let us know which requests we may make
    • We can use the browser to make requests and view the response

    Attribution

    Content from terminal and Making Connections

    Last updated on 2026-10-13 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 40 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What tools aside from the browser can I use to make API requests?
    • How can I authenticate myself?

    Objectives

    • Create an API token in the eLabFTW GUI
    • Make a basic call to the eLabFTW API using the command line and curl
    • Make user-specific API calls using the command line and curl and the API token

    Command-Line Interface

    Using our browser isn’t exactly useful when we want to automate workflows.

    A useful, built-in tool is a command-line interface, terminal, prompt, shell, and so on. The terminology is rather specific to operating system and often used interchangeably. We’re going to use terminal in the remainder of this course.

    Open a new terminal in Jupyter Lab. (Hint: if you already have a window open, use the blue + button in the top left corner of the Jupyter Lab window to open a new launcher. Then click the terminal icon.)

    We will use a tool called cURL to make API calls. This is a typical tool used for data transfer.

    We could head to its documentation to learn how to use it, but let’s be lazy and use what we already have.

    Head back eLabFTW’s API docs. Choose the HTML doc (v2).

    Similar to the Swagger page we saw in the previous episode, you will see the available endpoints on the left-hand pane, but now we have programmatic examples alongside them.

    Scroll to the Experiments section on the left and click postExperiment. On the right, cURL has already been selected in the example window. Let’s use this to programmatically create and experiment:

    1. Copy the text in the example window into a text editor in Jupyter Lab.
    2. Edit the required info
      1. Create a token
        1. Head your eLabFTW instance
        2. click your initials on the top right-hand side
        3. click settings
        4. Select the API KEYS header
        5. Under Create new key, enter a name for your key and select Read/Write from the permissions drop-down menu.
        6. click Generate an API Key
        7. Copy and paste this to the .env file in your workshop_data/research_computer folder. It will only be shown once!
      2. Copy and paste your token to the terminal, replacing [[apiKey]]
      3. Replace https://elab.local:3148 with your eLabFTW URL
      4. Add experiment info using the template below. Once done, add -d '{"title":"my api exp"} (replace info in curly brackets with full info)
      5. Copy and paste into your terminal
      6. Hit enter to run

    Template for data:

    Feel free to modify!

    JSON 

    {
   "title": "Temperature calibration",
   "body": "<p>Calibration check for the temperature sensor before the measurement run.</p><p>Expected range: 20-25 degrees C.</p>",
   "canread_base": 30,
   "canwrite_base": 20,
   "canread": "{\"teams\": [], \"users\": [], \"teamgroups\": []}",
   "canwrite": "{\"teams\": [], \"users\": [], \"teamgroups\": []}",
   "metadata": {
      "extra_fields": {
         "sample_id": {
            "type": "text",
            "value": "TC-2026-001"
         },
         "instrument": {
            "type": "text",
            "value": "Omega HH506RA"
         },
         "run_number": {
            "type": "number",
            "value": 1
         },
         "target_temperature": {
            "type": "number",
            "value": 22
         },
         "calibration_status": {
            "type": "select",
            "value": "planned"
         }
      }
   }
}

    Final code:

    BASH 

    curl -s -i -X POST \
    -H "Authorization: YOUR_TOKEN" \
    -H "Accept: application/json" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{
   "title": "Temperature calibration",
   "body": "<p>Calibration check for the temperature sensor before the measurement run.</p><p>Expected range: 20-25 degrees C.</p>",
   "canread_base": 30,
   "canwrite_base": 20,
   "canread": "{\"teams\": [], \"users\": [], \"teamgroups\": []}",
   "canwrite": "{\"teams\": [], \"users\": [], \"teamgroups\": []}",
   "metadata": {
      "extra_fields": {
         "sample_id": {
            "type": "text",
            "value": "TC-2026-001"
         },
         "instrument": {
            "type": "text",
            "value": "Omega HH506RA"
         },
         "run_number": {
            "type": "number",
            "value": 1
         },
         "target_temperature": {
            "type": "number",
            "value": 22
         },
         "calibration_status": {
            "type": "select",
            "value": "planned"
         }
      }
   }
}' \
    "https://elab.parks.web.gateway.ionos.coscine.dev/api/v2/experiments"
    Callout

    You can type this info directly into your terminal. For larger requests, however, especially when just starting out, it can be difficult to navigate. Thus, copy and pasting from a text editor may be easier and it is easier to catch problems.

    Callout

    You can load the API key from the .env file instead of pasting the secret into the command. From the research_computer/ directory, run:

    BASH 

    set -a
source .env
set +a

    The .env file should contain ELAB_API_KEY and ELAB_API_HOST. The key is then available as the $ELAB_API_KEY environment variable. Use it in the request like this:

    BASH 

    curl -s -i -X POST \
   -H "Authorization: $ELAB_API_KEY" \
   -H "Accept: application/json" \
   -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
   -d '{"title":"my api exp"}' \
   "$ELAB_API_HOST/experiments"

    This keeps the token out of the command itself. Do not print the variable or share the .env file. If you believe you unsafely used an API key, always revoke it and create a new one.

    Challenge

    Challenge

    What would the command line cURL API call look like that retrieves the experiment we just created? Write and execute this command. Then, analyze the response and see if everything is as you imagined.

    Hint: use the experiment ID in the response from your last API call when building the URL for the request.

    The POST response includes the URL of the new experiment in its Location header. Copy the experiment ID from that URL, then use it in a GET request:

    BASH 

    curl -sS \
   -H "Authorization: $ELAB_API_KEY" \
   -H "Accept: application/json" \
   "$ELAB_API_HOST/experiments/<EXPERIMENT_ID>"

    This prints the JSON response directly in the terminal. The response should contain the experiment title and body, its creation and modification details, the permission settings, and the values in metadata.extra_fields.

    For more readable, indented JSON, you can pipe the response through jq:

    BASH 

    curl -sS \
   -H "Authorization: $ELAB_API_KEY" \
   -H "Accept: application/json" \
   "$ELAB_API_HOST/experiments/<EXPERIMENT_ID>" | jq .

    Here, | passes the response to jq, and . tells jq to display the complete JSON document. If jq is not installed, install it with one of these commands:

    BASH 

    # macOS with Homebrew
brew install jq

# Debian or Ubuntu
sudo apt install jq

# Windows PowerShell with winget
winget install jqlang.jq

    On Windows PowerShell, use curl.exe rather than curl to call cURL explicitly, because curl may be an alias for a PowerShell command (shortened example):

    POWERSHELL 

    curl.exe ... | jq .
    Challenge

    Challenge

    Fill in the blanks for the the script in research_computer/attach_measurement.sh to attach the measurement file (research_computer/measurement.csv) to the created experiment.

    This is an example of a bash script. There is both a commented and uncommented version. The commented version explains what each line does.

    Ensure your .env file is set up with your API token and the API host URL.

    Run the script with the experiment ID and the measurement file as arguments. For example:

    BASH 

    ./attach_measurement.sh 94 ./measurement.csv

    The upload endpoint expects multipart/form-data, so the file must be sent with -F. Make it executable with chmod +x attach_measurement.sh, and run it with the experiment ID and file:

    BASH 

    #!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd -- "$(dirname -- "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
ENV_FILE="${ENV_FILE:-$SCRIPT_DIR/.env}"

if [[ -f "$ENV_FILE" ]]; then
      set -a
      source "$ENV_FILE"
      set +a
fi

: "${ELAB_API_HOST:?Set ELAB_API_HOST in $ENV_FILE or the environment}"
: "${ELAB_API_KEY:?Set ELAB_API_KEY in $ENV_FILE or the environment}"

EXPERIMENT_ID="${1:?Usage: $0 EXPERIMENT_ID MEASUREMENT_FILE}"
MEASUREMENT_FILE="${2:?Usage: $0 EXPERIMENT_ID MEASUREMENT_FILE}"

curl_options=(
      -H "Authorization: $ELAB_API_KEY"
      -F "file=@$MEASUREMENT_FILE"
      -F "comment=Temperature calibration measurement"
)

UPLOAD_URL="$ELAB_API_HOST/experiments/$EXPERIMENT_ID/uploads"
curl -sS -f -i "${curl_options[@]}" "$UPLOAD_URL"
    Key Points
    • API tokens authenticate requests made from the command line
    • cURL can create, retrieve, and update data through the eLabFTW API
    • API responses contain JSON data and HTTP headers that help interpret the result
    • Environment variables and .env files keep API credentials out of commands
    • File uploads use the eLabFTW upload endpoint with multipart/form-data

    What is Python?

    Python is a high‑level, interpreted programming language that was created in the early 1990s by Guido van Rossum. It reads almost like plain English, which makes it especially attractive for people whose primary expertise is not computer science (e.g. biologists, chemists, physicists, engineers).

    When you run a Python script, the Python interpreter reads the source code line‑by‑line, translates it into byte‑code, and executes it on the fly – you do not need a separate compilation step.

    • Python gives you a clean, readable language that lets you focus on the scientific question rather than low‑level programming details.
    • Its extensive libraries let you go from raw data to publication‑quality figures in a few lines of code.
    • When performance becomes critical, you can combine Python with compiled extensions or off‑load heavy work to specialized tools.

    What is a Jupyter Notebook

    A Jupyter Notebook is an interactive web‑based document that combines executable code, rich text, plots, and multimedia in a single, linear layout.You open it in a browser, but the Python (or other language) kernel runs on your computer (or on a remote server) and evaluates each cell on demand. Core concepts

    • Cells – The notebook is divided into blocks called cells.

      • Code cells contain Python (or R, Julia, …) statements that are sent to the kernel when you press Shift + Enter. The output—text, tables, images, interactive widgets—appears directly below the cell.
      • Markdown cells hold formatted text written in Markdown (headings, lists, links, LaTeX equations, etc.). They let you annotate your analysis, describe the rationale, or document results.

    • Kernel – A background process that executes the code. The notebook UI sends the cell’s source to the kernel, receives the result, and displays it. You can restart, interrupt, or switch kernels (e.g., Python 3, R) without leaving the notebook.

    • Output – Anything that a normal REPL would print can appear: plain text, JSON, tables, Matplotlib/Plotly figures, HTML, LaTeX‑rendered equations, or interactive widgets (sliders, drop‑downs).

    Crash course: Python Basics

    1. Printing & basic data types

    ::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: instructor note

    These will be live coded in a Jupyter notebook.

    PYTHON 

    # Print a greeting
print("Hello, eLabFTW researcher!")

# Numbers, strings, booleans, which can be stored in variables
my_int   = 42            # integer
my_float = 3.14          # floating‑point
my_bool  = True          # boolean

print(my_int, my_float, my_bool)

    Expected output

    Hello, eLabFTW researcher!
42 3.14 True

    2. Variables & dynamic typing

    PYTHON 

    a = 10          # a is an int
a = a * 2.5    # now a becomes a float (25.0)

print(a)

    Output

    25.0

    3. Lists (ordered collections)

    PYTHON 

    samples = ["S1", "S2", "S3"]   # create a list
print(samples[0])              # first element → "S1"

# Append a new sample name
samples.append("S4")
print(samples)

    Output

    S1
['S1', 'S2', 'S3', 'S4']

    4. Loop over a list (for‑loop) to create a dictionary

    PYTHON 

    results = {}
for sample in samples:
    results[sample] = len(sample)   # store the length of the name

print(results)

    {'S1': 2, 'S2': 2, 'S3': 2, 'S4': 2}

    5. Conditional statements

    threshold = 5
value = 7

if value > threshold:
    print("value is larger")
else:
    print("value is smaller or equal")

    Output

    value is larger

    6. Defining and calling a function

    PYTHON 

    def greet(name: str) -> str:
    """Return a friendly greeting."""
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

print(greet("Alice"))

    Output

    Hello, Alice!

    7. Reading and writing JSON files

    PYTHON 

    import json

payload = {"experiment": "test", "value": 123}

# Write to disk
with open("payload.json", "w") as fp:
    json.dump(payload, fp, indent=2)

# Read it back

    data = json.load(fp)

print(data)

    Challenge

    Challenge

    What will be printed?

    PYTHON 

    x = 5
x = "five"
print(x)

    A. 5
    B. five
    C. TypeError

    B – Python variables are dynamically typed; the second assignment overwrites the first.

    The eLabFTW Python API Library

    One of the advantages of Python is that there are many ready-made libraries that allow us to easily reuse code others have created for a specific purpose.

    For eLabFTW, there is elabapi-python. We can find information on it via the API docs selection page by clicking Python Library (v2).

    Here, we can find some examples and information such as installation. We will do something similar to what the page says and install it directly via our Jupyter Notebook:

    BASH 

    %pip install elabapi-python
    Callout

    This installs it directly in the environment we are working in so it is accessible to our notebook.

    To install it locally (e.g., if you are working outside of the Jupyter environment), open a terminal window and install via pip. This usually looks like:

    BASH 

    pip install elabapi-python

    However, your Python and pip installation may use pip3 instead of pip.

    As indicated by the elabapi-python installation instructions, it is highly recommended to work in a virtual environment. We recommend uv for creating and managing these:

    BASH 

    cd researcher_user
uv init --bare # initialize the project in the desired directory
uv add elabapi-python python-dotenv # add the API client and .env support
uv sync

    The package elabapi-python is imported as elabapi_python, and python-dotenv is imported as dotenv in client.py. Ensure you have added your credentials and the URL to a .env file.

    Once downloaded, we need to import the library into our notebook or scripts:

    PYTHON 

    import elabapi_python

    Python does not allow dashes, therefore, this is replaced with an underscore when calling the library.

    To get basic help on any Python library in Jupyter, we can use the help() function. For example, to get help on the elabapi_python library, we can run:

    PYTHON 

    help(elabapi_python)

    Honestly, for this specific case, the help output is not extremely helpful. However, it does give us some information on the library. We can also use the dir() function to get a list of all the functions in the library:

    PYTHON 

    dir(elabapi_python)

    To get started, we have the examples folder. Deltablot has created a nifty client configuration file. This has already been downloaded and included in your workshop_data dir.

    In the Python library, there are various clients that can be used to interact with the eLabFTW API. First, you set up the main one, which has already been done in client.py, then, you can create the others.

    Import this into your notebook using:

    PYTHON 

    from workshop_data.research_computer.client import api_client

    Let’s look at a couple examples in the GitHub repo.

    Check out 00_getting-started.py. We can see an info client:

    PYTHON 

    info_client = elabapi_python.InfoApi(api_client)
api_response = info_client.get_info()
print(api_response)

    In Jupyter Notebooks, we often get a pretty printed output, which is nice without using print(). This only works for the last line of a cell, so if you want to see the output of multiple lines or when using in a script, you will need to use print().

    PYTHON 

    api_response

    Similarly, we can see an experiment client:

    PYTHON 

    exp_client = elabapi_python.ExperimentsApi(api_client)

    Check out line 88, which shows us a get request. Remember how we created and retrieved an experiment in the CLI? Let’s try the same thing here using the experiment ID from the last lesson.

    PYTHON 

    exp_id = 94 # example: replace with your experiment ID
exp = exp_client.get_experiment(exp_id)
print(exp)

    You can see, this does the same things as we were doing before, but many of us find Python easier to read and understand than the CLI. This is especially true when we start to combine multiple steps into a single script.

    We can derive the code from the documentation, as well, which is a great way to learn how to use the API. Check out the API docs and click on Python Library (v2).

    Challenge

    Challenge

    What is the code for the client that interacts with resources in eLabFTW? Create this client in your notebook and use it to retrieve the resources from your eLabFTW instance.

    Hint: Look through the examples and keep your eyes out for a different word than resources.

    An example can be found in 05-create-modify-item in line 6:

    PYTHON 

    itemsApi = elabapi_python.ItemsApi(api_client)

    To retrieve and view all resources you have access to:

    PYTHON 

    resources = itemsApi.read_items()
resources
    Key Points
    • Jupyter Notebooks combine executable Python code, Markdown, and output
    • Python variables, collections, loops, conditionals, functions, and JSON support basic data workflows
    • The elabapi-python package provides Python clients for the eLabFTW API
    • A configured API client can be reused to access information, experiments, and resources
    • API documentation and examples help identify the appropriate client and method

    Content from Retrieving and Analyzing Data

    Last updated on 2026-10-13 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 90 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How can I retrieve experiment data with Python?
    • How can I analyze and visualize an attached data file?
    • How can I upload analysis results to eLabFTW?
    • How can I create and link experiments with Python?

    Objectives

    • Retrieve an experiment from eLabFTW using the Python package
    • Retrieve an attached data file from an eLabFTW experiment using the Python package
    • Use pandas and matplotlib to visualize downloaded data
    • Create an experiment using the Python API client
    • Upload analysis results to an experiment using the Python API client
    • Link experiments using the Python API client

    From an eLabFTW Experiment to a Plot

    In the previous episodes, we created an experiment and attached measurement.csv. Now we will reproduce the analysis workflow in an empty Jupyter Notebook:

    1. Retrieve the experiment and its attached file.
    2. Load the file into a pandas DataFrame.
    3. Create and interpret a plot.
    4. Upload the plot and an evaluation to eLabFTW.
    5. Create a combined analysis experiment and link it to the source experiment.

    Ask learners to use the experiment ID they created in the previous episode. If they do not have one, provide an accessible experiment ID from the workshop instance.

    Import the Client and Analysis Libraries

    The configured client, which we worked with in the previous episode, loads the API host and token from the .env file beside client.py. Keep the token in the environment and do not place it in notebook cells or output. Again, we import everything we need into out notebook:

    PYTHON 

    from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

import elabapi_python
from workshop_data.research_computer.client import api_client

    We have not worked with Pandas or Matplotlib yet, but they are the most common Python libraries for data analysis and visualization. We will use them to load the CSV file and create a plot.

    Also note, we use aliases for the libraries to make the code more concise. This is a common practice in Python, especially for frequently used libraries. pd is the standard alias for pandas, and plt is the alias for matplotlib.pyplot.

    Next, we create the API clients we need:

    PYTHON 

    experiments_api = elabapi_python.ExperimentsApi(api_client)
uploads_api = elabapi_python.UploadsApi(api_client)
links_api = elabapi_python.LinksToExperimentsApi(api_client)

    Retrieve an Experiment

    Use the experiment ID from the previous episode to retrieve your experiment. The response is an object containing the experiment metadata, body, links, and upload metadata.

    PYTHON 

    experiment_id = 94  # replace with the ID from the previous episode
experiment = experiments_api.get_experiment(experiment_id)

print(experiment.title)
print(experiment.body)

    We use the uploads API to interact with the attached files. Inspect the attached files before downloading anything. This gives you a better idea of the structure of the returned data:

    PYTHON 

    uploads = uploads_api.read_uploads("experiments", experiment_id)

for upload in uploads:
    print(upload.id, upload.real_name, upload.comment)

    The API distinguishes between upload metadata and the file contents. Select the measurement file and request its contents in binary format:

    PYTHON 

    measurement_upload = next(
    upload for upload in uploads if upload.real_name == "measurement.csv"
)

response = uploads_api.read_upload(
    "experiments",
    experiment_id,
    measurement_upload.id,
    format="binary",
    _preload_content=False,
)

measurement_path = Path("measurement.csv")
measurement_path.write_bytes(response.data)
    Callout

    The _preload_content=False argument is needed by this generated client when downloading file content. Without format="binary", the request returns upload information rather than the file itself.

    Analyze and Visualize the Data

    Load the downloaded CSV file and inspect its structure before plotting. This is where we will use Pandas to create a DataFrame from the CSV file. You can use the parse_dates argument to automatically convert the timestamp column to a datetime type:

    PYTHON 

    data = pd.read_csv("measurement.csv", parse_dates=["timestamp"])
data.head()

    Now, we will use matplotlib (plt) to create a first plot of temperature over time:

    PYTHON 

    ax = data.plot(
    x="timestamp",
    y="temperature_c",
    marker="o",
    title="Temperature calibration",
    ylabel="Temperature (°C)",
    xlabel="Time",
    legend=False,
)
ax.grid(True)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

    Ask learners to write a short interpretation in a Markdown cell. For example:

    The temperature increases slightly during the measurement period, from 21.8 °C to 22.1 °C. No abrupt changes are visible.

    Save the plot so it can be attached to the source experiment:

    PYTHON 

    plot_path = Path("temperature_plot.png")
fig = ax.get_figure()
fig.savefig(plot_path, dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")

    Upload the Analysis Result

    The Python client uses the same upload endpoint as the cURL command from the previous episode. The entity type is experiments and the entity ID is the experiment receiving the file.

    PYTHON 

    notebook_path = Path("analysis_notebook.ipynb") # this notebook

uploads_api.post_upload(
    "experiments",
    experiment_id,
    file=str(plot_path),
    comment="Temperature calibration plot",
)

uploads_api.post_upload(
    "experiments",
    experiment_id,
    file=str(notebook_path),
    comment="Analysis notebook",
)

    Refresh the upload list to verify the result:

    PYTHON 

    for upload in uploads_api.read_uploads("experiments", experiment_id):
    print(upload.real_name, upload.comment)

    An evaluation can be added to the experiment body with patch_experiment:

    PYTHON 

    evaluation = """
<p>The temperature increased from 21.8 °C to 22.1 °C over the measurement period.
No abrupt changes are visible.</p>
"""

experiments_api.patch_experiment(
    experiment_id,
    body=elabapi_python.EntityEditable(bodyappend=evaluation),
)

    Create and Link an Analysis Experiment

    Lets’s create a separate experiment for the combined analysis. The API uses the EntityEditable model for experiment creation.

    PYTHON 

    analysis_experiment = elabapi_python.EntityEditable(
    title="Temperature calibration analysis",
    body="<p>Combined analysis of the calibration measurements.</p>",
)

experiments_api.post_experiment(body=analysis_experiment)

    The create endpoint does not return a complete experiment object in every client version. Retrieve the experiments again and use the ID of the newly created experiment. In a real workflow, prefer the ID from the response Location header when it is available.

    PYTHON 

    experiments = experiments_api.read_experiments()
for item in experiments[:5]:
    print(item.id, item.title)

    Use the returned ID:

    PYTHON 

    
analysis_experiment_id = 95  # replace with the newly created experiment ID

    Link the analysis experiment to the source experiment. The direction is important: here the source experiment receives a link to the analysis experiment.

    PYTHON 

    links_api.post_entity_experiments_links(
    "experiments",
    experiment_id,
    analysis_experiment_id,
    body=elabapi_python.ExperimentsLinksSubidBody(action="link"),
)

    Upload the combined plot or notebook to the analysis experiment:

    PYTHON 

    uploads_api.post_upload(
    "experiments",
    analysis_experiment_id,
    file=str(plot_path),
    comment="Combined analysis plot",
)
    Challenge

    Challenge

    Using a second experiment ID, adapt the code above to:

    • retrieve its attached measurement file,
    • create a plot with both measurements,
    • write a short interpretation in a Markdown cell,
    • upload the combined plot to a new analysis experiment, and
    • link the two source experiments to that analysis experiment.

    Use read_experiments or the experiment IDs from the previous episodes to select the source experiments. Retrieve each file with UploadsApi, load the files into pandas, and combine them before plotting:

    PYTHON 

    experiment_ids = [94, 95]  # replace with the two source experiment IDs
frames = []

for source_id in experiment_ids:
    source_uploads = uploads_api.read_uploads("experiments", source_id)
    source_measurement = next(
        upload for upload in source_uploads if upload.real_name == "measurement.csv"
    )
    source_response = uploads_api.read_upload(
        "experiments",
        source_id,
        source_measurement.id,
        format="binary",
        _preload_content=False,
    )
    source_path = Path(f"measurement_{source_id}.csv")
    source_path.write_bytes(source_response.data)
    frame = pd.read_csv(source_path, parse_dates=["timestamp"])
    frame["experiment_id"] = source_id
    frames.append(frame)

combined = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)
combined.plot(x="timestamp", y="temperature_c", by="experiment_id", marker="o")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

    The remaining steps are the same: create an analysis experiment, upload the combined plot, and call post_entity_experiments_links for each source experiment.

    Key Points
    • The Python client can retrieve experiment metadata and attached files
    • pandas can turn downloaded CSV data into a table ready for analysis
    • matplotlib can visualize measurements and save plots for upload
    • The API client can create experiments, upload files, and append evaluations
    • Experiment links make the relationship between source data and analysis explicit
